rationale: Switch from the referential montage to the clinical 18-channel neonatal double-banana bipolar montage, band-pass filtered at 0.5–30 Hz, before computing the existing features. Bipolar derivations cancel the shared reference and widespread artifacts, so focal, low-amplitude rhythmic discharges stand out locally. The filter removes DC drift and line noise that currently swamp the line-length and band-power features.

Background EEG amplitude and spectrum vary a lot between neonates, so absolute log-power and line-length values from one baby don't transfer to another. I'm adding per-recording robust-normalized copies of every feature: subtract the recording's median and divide by its interquartile range (IQR). The model can then spot seconds that stand out from that neonate's own background, and it still sees the absolute values. This uses no labels.

Neonatal seizures differ from background and artifacts mainly in how rhythmic they are, and that's something amplitude and band power can't show. I'm keeping all 12 existing features unchanged and adding three rhythmicity measures per channel, each summarised across channels by max, median and min:

Neonatal seizures last at least 10 s and build up over time, but the classifier currently judges each second only from its own 8 s window. I'm adding centred moving averages of all 21 features over 15 s and 61 s windows, computed within each recording and without labels. This lets the model use temporal context: whether a rhythmic episode is sustained, and how this second compares with recent activity.

Neonatal seizures are focal, so pooling features across channels before classifying (max/median) mixes the one involved channel with background from the others. I'm switching to the classic per-channel detector (Temko/Tapani style). Each channel-second becomes its own sample: the channel's 9 features, the across-channel median of each feature as spatial reference, and 15 s and 61 s context. Training uses the recording-level label and subsamples seconds at stride 3 while keeping every seizure second. The second's probability is the max over channels, followed by the same 10 s smoothing.

With only about 60 training neonates and heavily autocorrelated seconds, the default gradient booster (min 20 samples per leaf, plus early stopping on a random split across seconds of the same recordings) can memorise patterns specific to individual neonates. I'm switching to a strongly regularised, deterministic booster so it learns patterns that transfer to unseen neonates: large leaves (min 1000 seconds), fewer leaf nodes, L2 penalty, a lower learning rate and a fixed number of iterations.

Background EEG changes a lot between neonates and also drifts within a recording (sleep state, medication, electrode impedance). Round 2's whole-recording normalization didn't help. This round adds features that compare each second with its own recent background instead: for each of the 21 per-second features, the difference from a centred 10-minute running median, plus a 15 s average of that difference. The running median is robust to seizures shorter than about 5 minutes, so a local rise in rhythmicity or power stands out even in low-amplitude or noisy recordings. All existing features stay unchanged and no labels are used.

Right now the running-median background is computed only after pooling across channels. A channel that is noisy all the time, or has high amplitude, therefore controls the max, and a focal, low-amplitude seizure in one quiet channel never stands out. This change keeps the 9 features for every channel. Each channel's features are compared with that channel's own centred 10-minute running median. Only then are they pooled across channels (max and median), so a focal rise above each electrode's own background can be detected. The 21 existing features stay unchanged, and no labels are used.

I'm adding a second, stacked stage that learns temporal context on top of the first-stage per-second probabilities. Stage 1 now makes out-of-fold predictions using 3 inner folds grouped by neonate, and the 3 inner models are averaged to score the test recordings. Stage 2 is a small, regularised booster. It sees the stage-1 logit smoothed over 5–121 s, running maxima, and how each second compares with that recording's own probability distribution (median and 99th percentile, computed without labels). The aim is to suppress short isolated false alarms, reward sustained evolving events, and calibrate across neonates, many of whom have no seizures. All of this matters for concatenated AUROC.

Neonatal seizures are focal and spread to neighbouring electrodes, while artifacts tend to hit either one electrode or every channel at once, so pooling with max/median loses that spatial pattern. This round adds 13 new per-second spatial features: the across-channel spread (std) of each of the 9 per-channel features; the fraction of channels that are strongly rhythmic; and the correlation of the 0.5–10 Hz signal after switching to an average reference (all channels and neighbours only, plus neighbours of the most rhythmic channel). The existing 21 features, context and background features are kept as they are.

The current gradient-boosting model picks its stopping point from a random split of seconds, and those seconds are highly autocorrelated within each recording, so it gets almost no signal about how well it generalises to new neonates. Since the score is entirely neonate-independent, I'm replacing the single model with a cross-validated bag of LightGBM models: each one trains on 3 of 4 neonate-grouped folds and is early-stopped on AUROC of the held-out neonates, and the 4 models' probabilities are averaged. This picks model size by how well it transfers to unseen babies and reduces dependence on individual training neonates.

This round adds 5 per-second features describing the frequency of the dominant rhythm: the 0.5–8 Hz spectral-peak frequency and the autocorrelation-peak frequency of the most rhythmic channel, the median and spread of the peak frequency across channels, and the fraction of channels at the same frequency as the most rhythmic channel. All existing features stay unchanged. Neonatal EEG often contains rhythmic artifacts at a steady rate, such as ECG (about 2–2.7 Hz) and respiration (about 0.5–1 Hz). Our current rhythmicity features fire on these artifacts as well as on seizures. Seizure frequency drifts and spreads to neighbouring electrodes, so the frequency features should help separate the two, especially once the existing context and running-median deviation features are applied to them.

The current features stop at 30 Hz, so a muscle, movement or electrode artifact that looks rhythmic in the 0.5–10 Hz band can't be told apart from a seizure. Such artifacts are likely a major source of false alarms in neonates without seizures. I'm adding 5 artifact-indicator features: high-frequency EMG power (30–100 Hz, excluding the 45–55 Hz mains band; max and median over channels), line-noise power at 49–51 Hz (median), and the EMG power and 0.5–8 Hz-to-EMG power ratio of the most rhythmic channel, so the model can check whether its rhythmicity is clean or contaminated. All existing features, context, background and smoothing stay unchanged.

Seizure burden in the Helsinki cohort is very uneven: a few neonates have long runs of seizures and supply most of the positive seconds. The booster is therefore learning those few neonates' seizure patterns and backgrounds, which hurts on unseen babies. This round reweights training seconds per neonate and per class by 1/sqrt(count), with each class's total weight kept unchanged, so every neonate's seizures and background count more evenly. Features, model and smoothing are unchanged.

rationale: Last round crashed because `featurize` changed what it returned. This round keeps `featurize` exactly as in the best solution and retries the same untested idea: each training recording is one neonate, so seconds are reweighted per recording and per class by 1/sqrt(count), with each class's total weight unchanged. That stops the few neonates with very long seizures from dominating what the booster learns.

Rhythmic neonatal seizure discharges are much more predictable than background or artifacts, and their spectral shape is simpler. I'm adding three classic signal-regularity features per channel (Temko/Tapani style): Hjorth mobility and complexity from the 0.5–30 Hz spectral moments, and the normalised prediction error of an order-8 linear model fitted on the 0.5–10 Hz signal at 32 Hz. All three are pooled with the existing rhythmicity summaries (max/median/min across channels plus spread), and every existing feature, context, background and smoothing step is unchanged.

Neonatal seizures are usually unilateral and regional, while state changes and most movement or ECG artifacts are symmetric across the head. The current pooling (max, median, std) keeps how much channels differ but not whether the difference follows a left-versus-right hemisphere pattern. This round adds 19 per-second hemispheric asymmetry features: for each of the 9 per-channel features, the largest left−right difference across the 8 homologous electrode pairs and the absolute difference between hemisphere means, plus the mean 0.5–10 Hz correlation between homologous pairs. All existing features, context, background, model and smoothing stay unchanged.

I'm adding 18 regional focality features. Each of the 9 per-channel features is averaged over each electrode and its 10-20 neighbours, then I take the maximum regional value and how far it sits above the median region (max minus median). Round 17's asymmetry gain suggests spatial pattern matters. Neonatal seizures involve a cluster of neighbouring electrodes, while single-electrode artifacts hit one channel and state changes hit all channels. Regional pooling should therefore boost coherent focal discharges and dilute isolated bad channels. All existing features, context, background, model and smoothing stay unchanged.

Round 1 used the bipolar montage instead of the referential features, and that hurt. This round keeps every existing feature and also computes the same 9 per-channel features on the 18-channel neonatal double-banana montage, pooled as max and median across derivations. Bipolar derivations cancel the shared reference and widespread artifacts, so this adds a second view of focal discharges at little extra cost. The bipolar spectra are obtained by subtracting the existing per-channel FFTs, so no new transforms are needed.

I'm averaging the single gradient booster with an ExtraTrees forest that uses large leaves and random split thresholds, then applying the same 10 s smoothing. The booster early-stops on a random split of highly autocorrelated seconds, so it can latch onto patterns specific to individual training neonates. A low-variance randomized forest on the same features should make errors that differ from the booster's, so averaging them should transfer better to unseen neonates.
